title: The Gift of the Magi

teacherSummary.text: On Christmas Eve Della Young has only $1.87 to buy a present for her husband Jim. She sells her long, beautiful hair for twenty dollars and buys a platinum fob chain for Jim's prized gold watch. Jim comes home and reveals he has sold the watch to buy Della a set of tortoise-shell combs for her hair. The narrator calls the two foolish children but declares them the wisest of givers: they are the magi.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Gift of the Magi,” how does Henry show love measured by sacrifice? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Gift of the Magi, how does Henry develop the idea of love measured by sacrifice? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Gift of the Magi develops the idea of love measured by sacrifice. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Gift of the Magi (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of love measured by sacrifice. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Gift of the Magi suggests about love measured by sacrifice. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's irony and symbolism), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how O. Henry uses irony in The Gift of the Magi to complicate the reader's understanding of love measured by sacrifice. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Gift of the Magi within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of love measured by sacrifice responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Gift of the Magi alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of love measured by sacrifice follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Gift of the Magi and its treatment of love measured by sacrifice. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's irony and symbolism, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Gift of the Magi as evidence for a larger claim about love measured by sacrifice in The Gift of the Magi. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Gift of the Magi as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of love measured by sacrifice. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Gift of the Magi.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What is the best gift you have ever given or received, and what made it special? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Nothing in this story needs a special warning.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are ransacking, cascade, depreciate, vestibule, accurate. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “She was ransacking the stores for Jim’s present.” In this sentence it means: searching a place thoroughly, often roughly. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of The Gift of the Magi would have known. O. Henry wrote the story in 1905 for the New York Sunday World. A flat at $8 a week and a $20 salary cut place the Youngs among New York's struggling clerks. Why does this story matter? A classic of situational irony and a Common Core Appendix B grades 9–10 exemplar. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “While the mistress of the home is gradually subsiding from the first stage to the second, take a look at the home.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to love measured by sacrifice? I circle “mendicancy”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find irony, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: While the mistress of the home is gradually subsiding from the first stage to the second, take a look at the home. A furnished flat at $8 per week. It did not exactly beggar description, but it certainly had that word on the lookout for the mendicancy squad.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Irony, Symbolism, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how The Gift of the Magi develops the idea of love measured by sacrifice. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this story connect to sacrificial love? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Story quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the story quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this story suggests about love measured by sacrifice, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how irony shapes love measured by sacrifice. Tonight, read the next story and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.
